meta.note: All figures are monthly unless stated, in local currency (US = USD, Germany = EUR), and are informed estimates rounded for readability, not invoices. They are anchored to published cost-of-living indices and city rent data, then reviewed by hand. Each city carries the month it was last checked. Net-pay figures come from a simplified 2026 tax model and are estimates.

categories.label: Headline
categories.blurb: One shareable top-line: what a comparable single-person month of essentials costs in each city, converted to one currency.

categories.label: Housing
categories.blurb: Monthly rent for a one-bedroom in the city center, a one-bedroom outside the center, and a three-bedroom family apartment. German figures are cold rent (Kaltmiete), before heating and utilities.

categories.label: Groceries
categories.blurb: Estimated monthly grocery spend for a single person and for a family of four, buying a normal mix of staples and fresh food.

categories.label: Healthcare
categories.blurb: The structural difference matters more than the number. In the US this is a separate, variable cost outside your paycheck: a premium plus a deductible when you actually get sick. In Germany public health insurance is about 14.6 percent of gross income, split between you and your employer, and it is already taken out before your net pay lands.

categories.label: Transportation
categories.blurb: Owning and running a car (insurance, fuel, registration, upkeep, averaged monthly) versus a monthly public-transit pass. In Germany the Deutschlandticket covers nationwide regional and local transit for one flat monthly price.

categories.label: Utilities
categories.blurb: Electricity, heating, and home internet for a typical apartment. German electricity is among the most expensive in Europe, which narrows the gap most Americans expect here.

categories.label: Taxes and net income
categories.blurb: Enter a gross annual salary and see estimated take-home pay in each place. This is the category that surprises Americans the most: German gross pay looks similar, but a much larger slice comes off the top, most of it mandatory insurance rather than tax.

categories.label: Context notes
categories.blurb: Plain-language caveats: the currency date, what is an estimate, and the things that do not translate one to one.
